FY 2022 Projects

Green Infrastructure in the Illinois River Watershed

Project #: 22-100

Lead Project Partner: Illinois River Watershed Partnership

2023

Status: Active

Low Impact Development (LID) and Green Infrastructure (GI) practices are cost-effective ways to address NPS pollution challenges, and their implementation in Northwest Arkansas is of increasing importance. The frequency and duration of heavy-to-severe rain events has been increasing in recent years and urban development in the region continues to grow. The Illinois River Watershed, particularly, has seen a quarter of the watershed developed in the last 30 years, with 74% of soils considered moderately to extremely erodible. Over the next 3 years, IRWP and partners will construct, maintain, and demonstrate a number of BMPs in priority cities, including Rogers, Fayetteville, Siloam Springs, Bentonville, and Springdale. The project’s BMPs include detention basin retrofits, rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavement, vegetated roofs, and green-designed streets.

L’Anguille River Watershed Cost-Share

Project #: 22-200

Lead Project Partner: St. Francis County Conservation District

Status: Active

The L’Anguille River is listed as an impaired waterway on ADEQ’s 2018 303(d) List with concerns regarding sedimentation, turbidity, pesticides, and nutrient levels cited. Farmers in the area can help reduce these concerns by implementing BMPs on their properties. Row crop agriculture makes up the majority of land use within the watershed in St. Francis County, including Crowley’s Ridge. This project seeks to implement BMPs on at least 10 farms or around 8,050 acres. Targeted farms for the program are ones not funded by EQUIP or other cost share programs.

Enhancement and Establishment of River, Riparian, and Wetland Restoration in Northwest Arkansas

Project #: 22-300

Lead Project Partner: Watershed Conservation Resource Center

Status: Active

The Watershed Conservation Resource Center (WCRC) has successfully conducted 21 river and stream restoration projects in the Beaver Lake, Illinois River, Little Sugar, and Elk River Watersheds since 2008. However, once the initial stages of a restoration project are completed, maintenance and establishment of vegetation continue to be ongoing processes. To protect initial investments and ensure long-term success of sediment and nutrient reductions in the fast-growing region of Northwest Arkansas, WCRC will enhance 5,000 feet of river and riparian areas and 3 acres of wetlands at existing restoration sites.

Preserving Water Quality in the Beaver Lake Watershed

Project #: 22-400

Lead Project Partner: Northwest Arkansas Land Trust

Status: Active

Situated in the Ozark Highlands, Beaver Lake supplies over 350,000 residents with drinking water and provides ample recreational, tourism-related, and aesthetic value to the area. However, the urban centers of Northwest Arkansas continue to grow, and development is expanding into rural areas with few planning codes and ordinances concerning water quality. While the Beaver Lake Watershed has over 60% forest cover, which protects water quality, development is expected to accelerate forest conversion, jeopardizing water quality. The Northwest Arkansas Land Trust aims to protect high-quality forest land in the watershed through promoting the use of conservation easements and BMPs. Their goal is to complete 3 conservation easements or permanently protect 500 acres using conservation easements (whichever is greater) by the end of their 3-year project.

Smart Growth for Source Water Protection in the Beaver Lake Watershed

Project #: 22-500

Lead Project Partner: Beaver Watershed Alliance

Status: Active

The Beaver Lake Watershed Protection Strategy recommends the use of Low Impact Development (LID) projects to reduce nonpoint source pollutants. The term “Smart Growth” refers to a variety of development and conservation techniques that aim to protect human health and the natural environment. Rapid urbanization and the subsequent increase of impervious surfaces result in higher volumes of rainwater runoff, to which communities will have to adapt stormwater management strategies. LID and Smart Growth are complementary strategies that the Beaver Watershed Alliance intends to implement in order to address this issue. Three projects, including one with the City of Fayetteville, one with the City of West Fork, and one TBD, will utilize practices such as rain gardens, bioswales, and pervious pavers to improve infrastructure that better addresses the stormwater management needs of the people and of the environment. Since Smart Growth is not yet commonly heard of or practiced, these sites will also serve as educational sites to be toured by targeted stakeholders. Additionally, multiple forums on LID and Smart Growth will be held along with the development of resources such as brochures and signage. The project is expected to be completed October of 2025.

Implementation of Mullins Creek Restoration – Phase III

Project #: 22-600

Lead Project Partner: Watershed Conservation Resource Center

Status: Active

Mullins Creek is a headwater stream in the West Fork White River watershed and flows through the University of Arkansas campus in Fayetteville. Phase III of the Mullins Creek Restoration Project will build on Phases I and II, in which upstream areas and tributary Bulldog Branch were successfully restored. In addition to stream restoration, Phase III will include implementation of LID to retrofit an impervious parking lot adjacent to the stream.

Lake Leatherwood Watershed Assessment

Project #: 22-700

Lead Project Partner: Eureka Springs Parks and Recreation

Status: Active

For over 80 years, Lake Leatherwood has been enjoyed and cherished by Eureka Springs tourists and residents alike. Originally created by impounding Leatherwood Creek, a major tributary in the White River Watershed in order to collect sediment and provide recreation opportunity, Lake Leatherwood has since lately become inundated with high levels of bacteria, accumulated sediment, and invasive aquatic vegetation. Lake Leatherwood City Park is managed by Eureka Springs Parks and Recreation, who, in cooperation with the Watershed Conservation Resource Center, will be conducting a watershed assessment of the lake and West Leatherwood Creek. The project will assess the source of sediment, form a planning team, and develop rehabilitation solutions to address problems with the Lake. The planning project is expected to be completed by January 2026.

Water Quality Monitoring in the Upper Illinois River Watershed and Upper White River Basin

Project #: 22-800

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Water Resources Center

Status: Active

Land use in both the Illinois River and Upper White River Basin (also known as Beaver Reservoir) Watersheds have drastically changed in the past couple of decades. Much of what once was pasture and forest is being converted into an urban landscape. Both watersheds also flow into neighboring states of Oklahoma and Missouri, respectively, and are therefore the subject of trans-boundary water quality issues. Therefore, monitoring in these two watersheds is critical to understanding how land use changes are affecting water quality and identifying issues early on. The Arkansas Water Resource Center will be conducting water quality monitoring and data analysis across a total of 15 sites across both watersheds. Parameters measured include but are not limited to nitrate-nitrogen, chloride, sulfate, total phosphorus, total nitrogen, turbidity, and conductivity. The project is set to conclude December 2025.

Little River Watershed Outreach Education and WMP Implementation

Project #: 22-900

Lead Project Partner: UA Cooperative Extension Service

Status: Active

The Little River Watershed Management Plan and the 2018-2023 NPS Pollution Management Plan call for education and outreach as strategies to reduce nonpoint source pollution in the watershed. The Lower Little River Watershed was identified for the first time in the 2018-2023 NPS Pollution Management Plan as a priority watershed based on a qualified risk assessment. The watershed spans parts of the Ouachita Mountains and the Gulf Coastal Plain and includes four major reservoirs, including DeQueen, Gillham, Dierks, and Millwood Lakes. Segments of the watershed are impaired due to metals, pH, dissolved oxygen, bacteria, turbidity, and nutrients. The majority of the watershed is rural, with potential sources of pollution including livestock, poultry operations, cropland, unpaved roads, septic systems, and streambank erosion. Education about BMPs to reduce NPS pollution could be viable solution. The Sevier County Extension Service will conduct educational programs for municipal leaders, home and business owners, landowners, and agricultural producers in hopes to curtail the issue and increase awareness of BMPs in the watershed.

Lower Little River Watershed Unpaved Road Sediment Reduction and Fish Passage Assessment and Improvement

Project #: 22-1000

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission Stream Habitat Program

Status: Active

A large proportion of roads in Arkansas are unpaved, many of which include low water roads crossings that serve as sources of sedimentation and barriers to fish passage. In cooperation with the Arkansas Stream Heritage Partnership and the Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership, AGFC’s Stream Habitat Program has been surveying such low water crossings to evaluate the quality of structures and extent to which it prohibits animal stream crossing. This project will allow AGFC to prioritize barriers and remove them, along with restoring riparian corridors. This project will be completed by September 2025.

Watershed Management Plan for the Upper White River Watershed

Project #: 22-1100

Lead Project Partner: H2Ozarks (formerly known as Ozarks Water Watch)

Status: Active

Although the Upper White River Watershed has been an NPS Program priority watershed since 1998, there has yet to be an EPA 9 Element Plan that addresses the entire 8-digit HUC. The 9 Element Plan will include all 12-digit HUC sub-watersheds within or partially within Arkansas. The completion of a 9 Element Plan would allow stakeholders to apply for future NPS Program projects within the entire watershed. This project is expected to be completed by March 2024.

Frog Bayou / R. Pense Stream Bank Stabilization

Project #: 22-1200

Lead Project Partner: City of Fort Smith

Status: Active

Eroding banks of Frog Bayou Creek, located in the Boston Mountains of Crawford County, has annually contributed approximately 226,660 cubic feet of sediment to the stream for three years. The City of Fort Smith will install Bend-way weirs and stone toe protection and will re-slope eroding vertical banks to mitigate the issue. Expected sediment reduction totals approximately 225,000 cubic feet per year. The projected will be completed by December 2023.

Arkansas Silvicultural Nonpoint Source Project

Project #: 22-1400

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Department of Agriculture, Forestry Division

Status: Active

This project addresses statewide silvicultural BMPs. Sediment is a major cause of impact to streams resulting from silvicultural activities. The Arkansas Forestry Division has provided training and education programs to industry and private landowner stakeholders on BMPs to address NPS mitigation. This project will continue that education, as well as track and evaluate voluntary BMPs implemented across the state.

Upper Saline Watershed Modeling and Management Planning

Project #: 22-1500

Lead Project Partner: The Nature Conservancy

Status: Active

Approximately two-thirds of the Upper Saline Watershed are in the Upper West Gulf Coastal Plain, with the other third in the Ouachita Mountains. There are several waterbodies, including the Alum Fork, Cedar Creek, and Big Creek, among others, that have been identified as impaired in ADEQ’s 2020 303(d) List. Impairments include pH, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, and biological integrity. The EPA 9 Element Plan for the Upper Saline Watershed has not been updated since 2006. Because Arkansas Natural Resource Division uses an adaptive management approach, periodic evaluation of progress is required. This project will update the watershed model to reflect land use changes, and a new 9 Element Plan will be developed using the new model. The project will be completed by The Nature Conservancy in cooperation with the Arkansas Water Resource Center and the Saline River Watershed Alliance by December 2024.

FY 2023 – FY 2025 Projects

FY 2023 Projects

*Fiscal Year 2023 served as an administrative year, meaning the Natural Resources Division did not issue a Request for Proposals. As the program does not receive any state funding, the Nonpoint Source (NPS) Program utilizes every fifth year of 319(h) funding to fund the administrative capacity of the program. Additionally, this allows us to finalize projects and update the NPS Management Plan as we near the end of our 5-year cycle.

Nutrient Management Planning

Project #: 23-200

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Department of Agriculture

Status: Active

This project is an implementation of the State Water Quality Technician program for State Fiscal Years 2024 – 2026; July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. The Arkansas Department of Agriculture will execute subgrant agreements with conservation districts to develop nutrient management plans (NMPs). Each conservation district receiving State funding will employ personnel, provide equipment, supplies and other incidentals necessary to properly develop NMPs for poultry farms and other water quality activities within its service area.

Agricultural Water Quality Loan Repayments

Project #: 23-300

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Department of Agriculture

Status: Active

Arkansas Department of Agriculture, in conjunction with conservation districts and participating banks, provides low-interest loan money to agricultural landowners for installation of conservation practices that reduce nonpoint source pollution impacts.  This program is known as the Agricultural Water Quality Loan Program or SRF program.  The SRF program allows agricultural producers to secure low interest loans for the sole purpose of implementing practices that enhance water quality.  As the loans are repaid, the investment of the producer can be counted as non-federal match toward the 319(h) program.  The terms of the loans vary, but participants must agree to maintain the practice for the life of the loan and allow site inspections by NRCS.  Some of the common practices implemented through this program include tail water recovery systems, no till/minimum till, stacking sheds, exclusion fencing for cattle, land leveling and grade stabilization, and water control structures

Watershed Based Management Plan for the L’Anguille River Watershed

Project #: 23-400

Lead Project Partner: Olsson

Status: Active

The objective of this project is to prepare an update of the EPA-accepted nine element watershed management plan for the L’Anguille River watershed, while expanding local support for the plan and its implementation.

Middle Fork White River – Phase I: Assessment of Streambank Erosion and Stream Restoration Design

Project #: 23-1000

Lead Project Partner: Watershed Conservation Resource Center

Status: Active

The goal of the project is to evaluate areas of significant streambank erosion, quantify sediment and nutrient loads for the worst areas of erosion, and to develop a restoration plan for a one-mile length of unstable river within the Middle Fork White River watershed.

FY 2024 Projects

Water Quality Monitoring and Data Organization for Springs in the Northwest Arkansas Karst Region: Blowing Springs

Project #: 24-100

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Water Resources Center

Status: Active

This project will organize data of existing historic water quality and land use data for four springs in the Northwest Arkansas Karst region. This project will conduct water quality monitoring of selected springs under variable recharge and flow conditions. Historical data will be combined with project data to archive all available water-quality data from these springs.  Statistical techniques will be used to compare how water quality varies over time (e.g., Mann-Kendall Test) or between groups of water-quality data (e.g., analysis of variance with appropriate data transformations).

Hicks Creek-White River Watershed Protection Program

Project #: 24-200

Lead Project Partner: Baxter County Conservation District

Status: Active

This project aims to 1) Implement 150 Farm Plans on approximately 31,800 acres, resulting in the improvement of pasture conditions from “Fair to Worse” to “Good to Excellent”, 2) Treat 44 miles of stream and riverbank with voluntary livestock exclusion, 3) Complete three field days and/or demonstrations promoting the project.

Beaver Lake Watershed Streambank Erosion & Barrier Assessment, Stream Restoration Design, Implementation and Outreach for Watershed Planning

Project #: 24-300

Lead Project Partner: Beaver Watershed Alliance

Status: Active

This project aims to implement recommendations from the Beaver Lake Watershed Protection Strategy to reduce nonpoint source sediment and nutrient loads going into Beaver Lake and meet the goals of the Arkansas Nutrient Reduction Strategy through river system analysis, development of prioritization tools, development of restoration design, stream barrier removal, and technology transfer. Informed watershed planning will increase the success of sediment and nutrient loading reductions and restore aquatic and terrestrial habitats in the Beaver Lake watershed.

L’Anguille River Watershed – Water Quality Project

Project #: 24-400

Lead Project Partner: Cross County Conservation District

Status: Active

This project aims to promote and encourage implementation of the best management practices (BMPs) to target the ongoing problem of sedimentation from agricultural lands,  to inform land users of the detrimental effect the sedimentation is causing, and to emphasize BMPs available to reduce sedimentation and improve water quality in the L’Anguille River Watershed within Cross County.  The goal is to reduce sediment to the point that total maximum daily load goals are attained.

Water Quality Monitoring in Four Priority Watersheds; Bayou Bartholomew, Cadron, Little Red, and Lower White – Bayou Des Arc

Project #: 24-500

Lead Project Partner: Equilibrium

Status: Active

This project aims to collect, analyze, and report water quality data associated with nonpoint source pollution from strategic locations at or near the pour points of selected 12-digit hydrologic unit code watersheds for an evaluation of trends of current water quality and comparative to historical data.

Myatt Creek Sub-Watershed of the Spring River Watershed Basin

Project #: 24-600

Lead Project Partner: Fulton County Conservation District

Status: Active

The objective of this project is to ensure that water quality within the Myatt Watershed remains unimpaired. The Myatt Creek flows directly into the Spring River, and in order to maintain the integrity of the Spring River, education about the impacts to the watershed and implementation of best management practices can ensure that the Myatt Watershed will not be an impairment to the Spring River. 100 conservation plans are expected to be developed with Environmental Quality Incentive Program practices including brush management, herbaceous weed treatment, fencing, pasture and hay planting, livestock pipelines, heavy use areas, and watering facilities.

Mill Creek (Flatrock Creek) Conservation Practice Implementation

Project #: 24-700

Lead Project Partner: H2Ozarks

Status: Active

This project aims to work with landowners to implement conservation practices (CPs) designed to improve water quality as well as landowner economic benefits. This subwatershed of the Buffalo River Watershed (BRW) was identified as a recommended subwatershed for nonpoint source pollution control. However, little outreach and implementation efforts have focused on this portion of the BRW. This project will follow a current project aimed at outreach and education for landowners regarding the economic and environmental benefits of implementing CPs. Additionally, this project will leverage a current project fulfilling water quality monitoring activities to measure baseline water quality, as well as an anticipated project that extends that monitoring through the three years of this project duration. This will aid the goals/objectives related to this project proposal in the evaluation of changes in water quality related to the implementation of CPs.

White/Kings River Watershed Project

Project #: 24-800

Lead Project Partner: Madison County Conservation District

Status: Active

This project aims to maintain and improve the designated uses of the White and Kings River watersheds. 100 conservation plans covering approximately 25,000 acres will implement practices such as watering systems, cross fencing, pasture improvements, feeding area improvements, etc.

Streambank Restoration and Riparian Buffer Enhancement in the Upper Illinois River Watershed

Project #: 24-900

Lead Project Partner: Natural State Streams, LLC

Status: Active

This project aims to reduce nonpoint source pollution, following the Upper Illinois River Watershed Management Plan guidelines for reducing surface erosion (5.6.2.2). The project will consist of implementing natural channel design streambank restoration techniques (i.e. stone toe wall, wood-toe restoration, etc.), improving the riparian buffer through native plantings, and conducting volunteer days to educate the public on the importance of healthy riparian buffers.

Education on Regional Approaches to NWA Stormwater and Flood Management

Project #: 24-1000

Lead Project Partner: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture – Cooperative Extension Service

Status: Active

The goals of this project are to educate and engage elected officials (Mayors, City Council members, County Judges, Justices of the Peace), municipal staff, and planning officials (planning directors, planning commissioners, consultants) within the NWA urban corridor to improve stormwater and flooding management and decrease nonpoint source pollution in the Illinois River and Beaver Lake Watersheds.

Preserving Water Quality in the Illinois River Watershed

Project #: 24-1100

Lead Project Partner: Northwest Arkansas Land Trust

Status: Active

The primary goal of the project is to increase the acreage of priority lands in permanent protection through use of voluntary conservation easements and/or fee simple acquisition in the upper Illinois River watershed. The project will include one to three land protection projects in the watershed. Additionally, land trust staff will maintain public access and vegetation management focusing on invasive species management on existing protected preserves in the watershed using the properties as demonstration sites for the public.

Monitoring Sediment Transport from Unpaved Roads in Brush Creek

Project #: 24-1200

Lead Project Partner: Board of Trustees of the University of Arkansas acting for and on behalf of the University of Arkansas, Fayetteville

Status: Active

The project will monitor sediment and sediment-bound nutrient transport throughout the Brush Creek watershed, a key tributary to Beaver Lake, Northwest Arkansas’s key drinking water source. The Brush Creek watershed has majority unpaved roads, which can contribute excess nonpoint source pollutants, like sediment and sediment-bound nutrients, to Beaver Lake. Sites will be sampled throughout the Brush Creek watershed at baseflow and during high flow events to collect measurements of sediment and sediment-bound nutrient transport from unpaved roads. These monitoring efforts will help identify site characteristics to target for unpaved road best management practice (BMP) implementation, as well as direct state funding to implement unpaved road BMPs and reduce sediment and phosphorus loss to Beaver Lake.

Upper Cadron Creek Watershed Stream Barrier Remediation and Unpaved Road Erosion and Sediment Reduction

Project #: 24-1300

Lead Project Partner: The Nature Conservancy of Arkansas

Status: Active

The Nature Conservancy will work with partner Van Buren County to remove and remediate two aquatic organism passage barriers associated with high priority unpaved road crossings on Pine Mountain Creek and Grassy Creek in the Upper Cadron Creek watershed and implement erosion control measures to reduce nonpoint source sediment and nutrient loads entering Pine Mountain Creek, a tributary of Cove Creek and Cadron Creek. Aquatic organism passage and stream connectivity will be restored to Pine Mountain Creek and Grassy Creek, and sediment inputs and flooding during heavy rainfall events will be reduced by replacing the structurally failing, undersized and perched instream culverts with a bridge span and bottomless culverts designed to preserve the natural stream channel. Additional water quality improvements will be achieved through installing best management practices and improving adjacent unpaved roads to reduce sediment inputs to these tributaries of Cadron Creek, a state designated extraordinary resource waterway.

Using the Arkansas Watershed Stewardship Program to Increase Watershed Management Plan Implementation in Arkansas

Project #: 24-1400

Lead Project Partner: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture – Cooperative Extension Service

Status: Active

The goal of this project is to conduct Arkansas Watershed Stewardship trainings, establish water quality best management practice demonstrations, and engage in capacity building with watershed organizations and groups in Arkansas.

Natural Resources for Potential Development Sites

Project #: 24-1500

Lead Project Partner: Watershed Conservation Resource Center

Status: Active

This project aims to inform developers and development consultants such as civil engineering and architectural services providers about natural resource conservation opportunities associated with a potential development to be considered prior to or during conceptual design development.

Arkansas Unpaved Roads Program Support

Project #: 24-1600

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Department of Agriculture

Status: Active

This is a statewide program working in watersheds that have impairment due to sedimentation and other pollutants with half of the sites being in an Arkansas nonpoint source priority watershed or watershed with a 9-element plan.  Specifically, this project will act to augment the Arkansas Unpaved Roads Program demonstrating best management practices for unpaved roads.

FY 2025 Projects

Improving Water Quality in Karst Focal Areas of Northwest Arkansas

Project #: 25-100

Lead Project Partner: The Nature Conservancy

Status: Active

The Nature Conservancy will work with local non-profit groups and state agencies to implement recommendations from watershed management plans to reduce nonpoint source pollution in karst areas on both public and private lands throughout the Upper Illinois River and Upper White River Watersheds. Implemented practices will improve surface and groundwater quality and provide co-benefits for threatened and endangered species cave species. Funding will be used to provide cost share to private landowners for best management practices such as livestock exclusion fencing, critical area planting, riparian forest buffer, herbaceous weed control, karst sinkhole treatment, streambank and shoreline stabilization, stream habitat improvement and management, and other applicable practices identified as necessary. Once implemented, this project should result in the reforestation of 100 acres of floodplain, the stabilization of 500 linear feet of streambank, and the enhancement of 500 acres of terrestrial habitat, at least.

Growing Green: Cultivating Demand for Native Landscapes on the Illinois River Watershed

Project #: 25-200

Lead Project Partner: Illinois River Watershed Partnership

Status: Active

This project’s goal is to implement recommendations from the EPA-approved 2024 Watershed Management Plan through installation of 30 green infrastructure best management practices (BMPs), update the landowner database to effectively reach landowners in priority sub watersheds, and conduct education and outreach to landowners, cities, counties, landscapers, native plant growers and suppliers. The lead agency is the Illinois River Watershed Partnership, with support from Arkansas Department of Agriculture and EPA. Creating a comprehensive online resource hub along with an outreach campaign, promoting native plants through plant sales, and installing green infrastructure in targeted priority sub watersheds aims to foster widespread adoption of ecological landscaping practices while improving water quality through demonstrable BMP implementation.

Beaver Lake Watershed Flood Assessment, Smart Growth Implementation and Technical Assistance for Source Water Protection

Project #: 25-300

Lead Project Partner: Beaver Watershed Alliance

Status: Active

This project will implement recommendations from the Beaver Lake Watershed Protection Strategy to reduce nonpoint source sediment and nutrient loads going into Beaver Lake, meet the goals of the Arkansas Nutrient Reduction Strategy, and support the Arkansas Flood Plan by developing a HEC-HMS base model and flood assessment of the Beaver Lake watershed. The project also aims to implement three smart growth – low impact development projects and provide technical assistance to communities for smart growth initiatives. Informed watershed planning and project implementation will increase the success of sediment and nutrient loading reductions, restore aquatic and terrestrial habitats in the Beaver Lake watershed, and advance adoption of best management practices in local communities.

Arkansas Unpaved Road Education Project

Project #: 25-400

Lead Project Partner: Ozark Foundation

Status: Active

This project aims to (1) provide public education and outreach to relevant communities within prioritized watershed regions (as identified in the Arkansas Nonpoint Management Plan) focused on the preservation, maintenance and improvement of unpaved roads throughout the state, and (2) highlight and amplify existing Arkansas Department of Agriculture and other agency recommendations, policies, and education focused on the implementation of best management practices to reduce nonpoint source pollution in Arkansas.

Sediment Input Reduction within Wilburn Creek, a Major Tributary of the Little Red River

Project #: 25-500

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission

Status: Active

This project aims to address high streambank erosion rates, degraded riparian buffers, and lack of public awareness. The project involves the implementation of streambank stabilization structures, and riparian buffer enhancements on 1,000 ft of impaired banks along Wilburn Creek and increasing public awareness by volunteer planting opportunities and landowner workshops. The project will produce outputs like restoration plans and monitoring documentation. By reducing erosion, improving riparian buffer health, enhancing water quality, and educating the public, the project aligns with the Greers Ferry Tailwater Trout Management Plan. The project will be deemed successful if sediment contribution at the streambank stabilization structure locations is reduced by 80%.

Little Red River Watershed Cost Share

Project #: 25-600

Lead Project Partner: Buffalo Conservation District

Status: Active

This project aims to implement a program that will encourage voluntary participation of landowners and operators in applying best management practices (BMPs) within sub watersheds that contain or feed the Little Red River, and to implement recommendations from the Little Red River Watershed Management Plan to reduce sediment and nutrient loads going into Greers Ferry Lake. Water quality improvements will be achieved through the voluntary installation of natural design elements within the project area. The end goal of this project is to see implementation of BMPs on 8,500 acres of pastureland in the watershed.

Water Quality Monitoring in the Upper Illinois River Watershed and Upper White River Basin

Project #: 25-700

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Water Resources Center

Status: Active

The Arkansas Water Resources Center (AWRC) will conduct water quality monitoring within the Upper Illinois River and Upper White River watersheds, both of which are priority watersheds in the 2024-2029 nonpoint sources management strategy. The project will monitor at least 15 sites in each watershed for nutrients, sediment, and pathogens, among other water quality constituents, collecting an estimated 30 samples from each site. AWRC will analyze the samples in their lab and perform load estimations and trend analyses for the various sampling events. These monitoring data will add to the continuous data record in these important, sensitive watersheds allowing for long term trend analyses to be conducted.

Stream Barrier Remediation and Unpaved Road Erosion Reduction in the Upper Little Red River Watershed

Project #: 25-800

Lead Project Partner: The Nature Conservancy

Status: Active

This project aims to remove and remediate three high priority fish passage barriers on unpaved roads in the Little Red River watershed. In addition to restoring stream connectivity and aquatic organism passage to approximately 25 miles of stream network, this project will improve instream habitat and help reduce flooding during heavy rainfall events by replacing structurally failing, undersized and perched instream culverts with bottomless or partially submerged concrete box culverts designed to preserve the natural stream channel. The Nature Conservancy will implement erosion control measures to reduce nonpoint source sediment and nutrient loads entering the Little Red River. Water quality improvements will be achieved through installing best management practices and improving adjacent unpaved roads to reduce sediment inputs to the tributaries of the Little Red River, a state designated ecologically sensitive waterbody and extraordinary resource waterway.

Pilot Program: Establishing Riparian Buffers on Impacted Tributaries in the Buffalo River Watershed

Project #: 25-900

Lead Project Partner: Buffalo River Foundation

Status: Active

This project aims to reduce sediment, total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and other contaminants entering the Buffalo River and tributaries. The project involves the establishment of permanent riparian buffers to reduce erosion, reduce solar exposure and subsequently water temperature, and sequester carbon. The project will be eligible for properties throughout the Buffalo River watershed but will prioritize properties bordering impaired reaches or tributaries that contribute to impaired reaches in the watershed. The project will be deemed successful if 116 acres of riparian buffers are perpetually protected and if there is continued landowner interest in enrolling into the program; demonstrating that acquisition of conservation easements on riparian buffers is a viable option for reducing impairment within the watershed.

Implementation of Little Sandy Creek Restoration (Phase II)

Project #: 25-1000

Lead Project Partner: Water Conservation Resource Center

Status: Active

This project will complete Phase II of the stream restoration project on approximately 1,880 feet of the  Little Sandy Creek in the Illinois River Watershed near Johson, AR where accelerated erosion threatens critical infrastructure including power, sewer, gas, and water supply.  Phase I, funded in FY24 utilizing OSG funds, developed the engineering plans for the entire project and construction on 750 feet of streambank. In Phase II, the remaining 1,130 feet of streambank restoration will be completed, the site will be revegetated, post-construction water quality monitoring will be conducted, and the project will be used as an educational site for the public and for local municipal and county planning and engineering personnel.

Upper Saline River Watershed Project

Project #: 25-1100

Lead Project Partner: Saline County Conservation District

Status: Active

This project aims to implement recommendations from the updated Upper Saline River Watershed Management Plan to reduce nonpoint source sediment and nutrient loads entering the Saline River and its tributaries. Objectives include voluntary implementation of best management practices (BMPs), specifically NRCS 329 No Till and NRCS 345 Reduced Till, through the acquisition of a no-till seed drill for the Saline County Conservation District and enhanced education and outreach to promote implementation of BMPs throughout the watershed. A minimum of three field days supplemented with educational material will be held by the Saline County Conservation District aimed at reducing nonpoint source pollution.

Streambank Stabilization and Habitat Restoration for Ferndale Creek in Lower Arkansas Maumelle Watershed

Project #: 25-1200

Lead Project Partner: Ferncliff Camp and Conference Center

Status: Active

Ferncliff Camp and Conference Center will remove an aquatic organism barrier (dam) and restore connectivity to Ferndale Creek, a tributary of the Lower Arkansas Maumelle watershed. Once the dam is removed, water quality will be improved through streambank stabilization measures and the reestablishment of riparian revegetation along the channel. The project will have the secondary benefits of restored aquatic passage in the waterbody and is expected to be a great education resource, as the site will feature information kiosks that highlight the importance of riparian zones, habitat restoration, and aquatic connectivity to a diverse range of people that attend the facility. The restoration of this stream is also expected to relieve flash flooding issues that the site experiences.

Implementing Advanced Water Quality Monitoring in the L’Anguille River Watershed

Project #: 25-1300

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas State University

Status: Active

This project will allow Arkansas State University to monitor and assess nonpoint source pollution, nutrients, and other water quality parameters at multiple sites within the impaired L’Anguille River Watershed, including Hydrick Creek, Prairie Creek, Copper Creek, McFaran Branch, Black Fork, Lick Creek, Big Telico Creek, Outlet First Creek, Lower Second Creek, and Coffee Creek. The project will involve the collection and analysis of water samples for nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus), total suspended solids, turbidity, and basic water chemistry (temperature, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, and pH) to inform management strategies for reducing nonpoint source pollution and improving water quality in the watershed.

Middle Fork Little Red River Bank Stabilization/Sediment Reduction

Project #: 25-1400

Lead Project Partner: Arkansas Wildlife Federation

Status: Active

The primary objective of this stream restoration project is to stabilize approximately 1,584 feet of eroding streambanks along the Middle Fork Little Red River (MFLRR), just downstream of its confluence with Meadow Creek, a tributary of the MFLRR. This effort aims to reduce nonpoint source pollution by minimizing sediment and nutrient loading into the river. In addition to bank stabilization, the project will also focus on reestablishing a healthy riparian corridor. This will be achieved through active volunteer participation in native plantings, educational outreach, and the implementation of best management practices by local landowners.
